newsitem.title: FRANCE: French trawlers protest in forbidden Guernsey zone.
newsitem.headline: French trawlers protest in forbidden Guernsey zone.

text.p: French trawlers fished in a contested patch of water off the British Channel island of Guernsey on Monday as local officials stood by and took down their names for possible later action.

Daniel Lefevre, head of the Lower Normandy regional fishing committee, said by radio-telephone that about 10 French vessels had entered the zone declared by Guernsey to be off-limits to French fishermen shortly after 3 p.m. (1400 GMT).

Calling from one of the French vessels, he said that no British vessel had attempted to prevent them from entering the contested 12-mile-square zone -- known as the Sark Box -- or to prosecute them for having done so.

But the Guernsey sea fisheries vessel Access Challenger stood by observing the French vessels, and noted their names and registration numbers. At the same time, a Guernsey customs rigid inflatable moved swiftly from boat to boat.
Some of the French boats could clearly be seen fishing despite strong winds and 14-foot (four-metre) waves. Others simply steamed about the contested zone southeast of Guernsey.
The French coastguard cutter Coriandre stood by in case Guernsey fishermen or authorities attempted to board any French boats or arrest their crew.

The French fishermen are angry over Britain's decision to go back on a 1994 agreement granting them fishing rights in the Sark Box, and French officials said Paris was determined to retain fishing rights there.
"We do not want French fishing vessels to be prevented from entering this zone," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said in Paris.
"While we await the resumption of negotiations, expected in January, we want the status quo to be maintained," the spokesman said at a regular ministry news briefing.
Apart from the 10 vessels that arrived in the area, another 15 to 20 which had started out for the zone on Monday morning had turned back due to foul weather, Lefevre said.

Britain's decision to end the 1994 agreement was made last month, but Sunday was the first day that Guernsey authorities had said they would enforce the move by prosecuting French boats which entered the contested area.
However a British embassy spokeswoman said that French and British authorities had conferred at the weekend and agreed that the French boats could protest peacefully in the area.
"Both sides agree that the last thing we want is any incidents. Both sides would like negotiations to resume as soon as possible," she said.

Guernsey fishing authorities have already set out proposals for a new accord to replace the 1994 agreement, and the French have made counter-proposals, she said. "We now hope for early talks on a replacement regime," she said.
The 1994 agreement allowed French trawlers to operate in the island's waters in return for rights for Guernsey fishermen to fish in French waters.
But Guernsey recently concluded that the accord was not in its best interests and asked London to withdraw from it, which it subsequently did, the embassy spokeswoman said.
